thesis: During periods of extreme price compression, the statistical dependency between the normalized extreme of closing prices and the detection of new lows in absolute high prices suggests that when price action becomes exceptionally constrained relative to recent highs, it often precedes a breakout or breakdown. This relationship exists because the z-scored exponential of opening price momentum and the z-scored sigmoid of absolute highs both capture the intensity of price rejection and compression, where extreme normalization of closes signals latent volatility that manifests as new lows when high prices fail to sustain. The underlying mechanism is a regime shift from low-volatility compression to directional momentum, where the failure to establish new highs (captured by the new low in absolute highs) coincides with the statistical extremity of closing prices, revealing that markets tend to resolve extreme compression through momentum reversals that first appear in the failure to exceed prior highs.
